title: The ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
hook: he's lifted out of sight, and two men ask why they're staring at the sky

segments.voice: Yesterday, a charcoal fire on a beach and three questions: three denials, three loves.

A car pulls away. A hand waves from the back window until the corner; the street empties, and the person on the sidewalk keeps looking anyway. The Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. Acts says that after the empty tomb Jesus appeared to his friends for forty days. Gathered with him one last time, they ask what they've carried all along: is this the moment you restore the kingdom to Israel? He says the timing isn't theirs to know. Then, as they watch, he's lifted up, and a cloud takes him out of their sight. And they stand there, staring at the sky.
screen: `WAVING FROM THE BACK WINDOW.` → `FORTY DAYS.` → `A CLOUD TAKES HIM.`

segments.voice: Just before he goes, Jesus gives them the map of the whole book of Acts: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." Jerusalem first, then Judea's countryside, then Samaria, the neighbors with an old quarrel, then everywhere. Then he's gone, they're still looking up, and two men in white stand beside them. In the King James Bible: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" It's almost funny: the sky has just opened, and heaven's first words are, why are you still standing here? The men promise he'll come back the same way, and the disciples walk back down to Jerusalem, to wait and pray. Luke tells this scene twice, at the end of his Gospel and at the start of Acts. Nothing in the text suggests a trip into outer space. In the Bible a cloud is an old sign of God's presence, from the cloud over Sinai to the bright cloud on the mountain of light, and the churches' old creeds say that he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father: Jesus taken fully into God's presence, not gone for good. Christians differ on how literally to picture the rising, and the text doesn't say how it looked. Many churches keep Ascension Day forty days after Easter, on a Thursday, though some move it to the Sunday after. But the heart of the story is the question. Stop staring. Go.
screen: `JERUSALEM, THEN THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `WHY STAND YE GAZING?` · `A CLOUD MEANS GOD IS NEAR.` · `FORTY DAYS AFTER EASTER.` · then, large: `STOP STARING. GO.`

segments.voice: At a window or outside if you can, look up at whatever's there, sky, ceiling, clouds, and let it be big; if you pray, let that be your prayer, without words. Then bring your eyes down slowly to what's in front of you, a street, a room, a person, a sink full of dishes, the kind of place the disciples were sent back to, and notice one thing there that needs you.
The ascension. Jesus taken up out of sight, forty days after Easter, and his friends sent back down the hill.
Your line: stop staring; go. Tomorrow, wind and fire in Jerusalem. That was day seventy-four.

howItsDone: Many churches celebrate Ascension Day on the Thursday forty days after Easter, and Christians confess in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds that Jesus ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.

original.note: Greek: a taking up. Luke uses it for his being received up, and Greek-speaking churches name the feast with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus floats off into space.
what it means: he's taken into God's presence, and the first thing heaven says to his friends is, why are you still staring? go.
what a scholar hears: Luke tells it twice (Luke 24 and Acts 1), and the cloud echoes the cloud of God's presence in Exodus and at the transfiguration.
recall: remembering that makes the past present
